strengths: The paper tackles a timely and under-served problem: object-level change detection under viewpoint variation in multiview videos. The proposed task is clearly motivated by robotics and monitoring applications, and it is a meaningful extension beyond near-duplicate-view change detection.

Although no formal contribution type is declared, the strongest contribution is best viewed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than only Algorithms/General. Under that lens, SceneDiff Benchmark is valuable: 350 real video pairs, 1009 changed objects, indoor/outdoor and egocentric subsets, instance masks across visible frames, change-type labels, and both per-view and per-scene evaluation protocols.

The evaluation protocol recognizes an important distinction between detecting per-frame regions and identifying changed physical objects across views. The per-scene AP and type-aware AP are useful metrics for the intended task and expose failure modes that per-view scores would hide.

The method is technically sensible and well matched to the task: joint feed-forward geometry, co-visible frame pairing, asymmetric depth reasoning, DINO feature comparison, SAM region pooling, 3D score aggregation, and cross-view association. The components are not individually radical, but their integration is coherent and effective.

Experimental evidence is broad for a benchmark/method paper. The authors compare against CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, VLM/GroundingSAM, RC-3D, and ChangeSim baselines; report ablations over geometry models, appearance backbones, and score cues; include runtime; and discuss failures such as cluttered repeated objects, limited overlap, and lighting changes.

Results support the main empirical claim that current alternatives struggle badly in this setting. SceneDiff improves substantially over baselines on the new benchmark and RC-3D, while the ablations show that both geometry alignment and appearance features are important.

The manuscript is mostly clear, well illustrated, and unusually candid about limitations. The supplementary material adds useful details about annotation workflow, baseline adaptations, threshold sensitivity, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The benchmark contribution would be stronger with more rigorous annotation quality evidence. The paper states that masks are reviewed and refined, but does not report inter-annotator agreement, audit statistics, label correction rates, or quantitative mask/instance consistency checks. For a dataset paper, this weakens confidence in ground-truth reliability.

The evaluation protocol is pragmatic but somewhat lenient and may overstate object detection quality. Converting predictions to centroids and checking whether they fall inside ground-truth boxes ignores mask quality and coarse localization error; allowing up to two detections per object without penalty is reasonable for ambiguity but can hide over-segmentation. This is in tension with the dataset’s dense instance-mask annotations.

Baseline comparisons are useful but not fully satisfying. Several baselines require substantial adaptation, some are only evaluated per-view, and 3DGS-CD is run with the authors’ regressed camera parameters and modified occupancy handling. These choices are explained, but they make it hard to separate intrinsic method superiority from differences in pipeline engineering and evaluation compatibility.

The method’s originality is moderate. It is a well-executed composition of strong pretrained models and hand-designed scoring/association rules rather than a fundamentally new learning or geometric formulation. This is acceptable for a benchmark-led paper, but less compelling if judged primarily as an algorithmic contribution.

Absolute performance remains limited, especially on the harder SD-K subset where per-scene AP is 20.9 and APtype is 12.2. The paper acknowledges that the task is far from solved, but some claims of robust detection should be tempered given these low type-aware results.

The benchmark scale is meaningful but still modest for modern vision datasets, especially with only 250 test pairs and 50 validation pairs per subset. It is unclear how diverse the manually collected scenes are in terms of geography, devices, camera quality, lighting, and object categories beyond the summary plots.

Reproducibility depends on the release of dataset, annotation tool, and code, which is promised but not available in the anonymous submission. The method also relies on recent large pretrained models, so exact versions, checkpoints, and compute/memory requirements should be specified more completely for replication.

The paper has only a light discussion of privacy and societal considerations. The data collection instructions mention avoiding identity information, but a benchmark built from real indoor/outdoor videos and egocentric kitchen footage would benefit from clearer consent, filtering, licensing, and privacy-handling procedures.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-served problem: object-level change detection across multiview captures with viewpoint variation, which is relevant to robotics, construction monitoring, and spatial scene understanding.

Although no explicit contribution type is declared, the strongest contribution is better viewed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General. Under that lens, the proposed SceneDiff Benchmark is a meaningful addition: 350 real video pairs, instance-level masks, changed-object attributes, and both per-view and per-scene evaluation are more useful than many prior change-detection datasets that assume near-identical viewpoints or provide only semantic labels.

The benchmark definition usefully distinguishes Added, Removed, and Moved objects and introduces per-scene evaluation, which is the right direction for multiview change detection because repeated per-frame detections should not be mistaken for object-level performance.

The method is sensible as a training-free composition of recent geometry, segmentation, and feature models. The paper gives reasonable ablations showing the importance of geometry model choice and appearance-feature reprojection, and it reports clear gains over the included baselines on the new benchmark and RC-3D.

The paper includes limitations and failure analyses, including cluttered repetitive scenes, geometry failure under low overlap, strong lighting changes, dynamic content, and ambiguous moved-object configurations. These discussions are useful and make the scope of the method clearer.
weaknesses: The scientific case is weakened by the evaluation protocol. The point-based metric converts predicted masks/boxes to centroids and allows up to two detections per ground-truth object without penalty. This may substantially overestimate object-detection quality, especially for methods that produce coarse or fragmented regions, and it does not directly measure mask quality despite the dataset containing dense instance masks.

The reported absolute performance is modest on the authors' own benchmark, especially on SD-K: per-scene AP is 20.9 and APtype is 12.2. This suggests that the method is far from robust, yet the paper's headline claims emphasize large relative improvements. The large relative gains partly reflect extremely weak baseline performance rather than a mature solution.

The baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. CYWS-3D lacks per-scene association, VLM+GroundingSAM is a fragile pipeline rather than a strong specialized baseline, and 3DGS-CD is modified with the authors' regressed camera parameters and evaluated under a setup where it appears ill-suited. More careful comparisons to recent correspondence/foundation-model change detection methods, stronger tracking/association baselines, and oracle-geometry variants would be needed to isolate what is genuinely novel.

The method itself is mostly an engineering assembly of existing foundation models: pi3 for geometry, SAM for regions, DINOv3 for features, thresholding, and feature/geometry-based association. The algorithmic novelty is limited, and many design choices, thresholds, and weights appear heuristic.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The dataset, annotation tool, and code are promised for release, but not available for review; several key dependencies are recent or potentially unreleased at submission time. The benchmark contribution depends heavily on annotation quality, split construction, and licensing/availability of HD-Epic-derived examples, but these aspects are not documented deeply enough in the main paper.

Dataset scale and diversity are useful but still limited for the breadth of claims. There are 50 scenes and 350 sequence pairs, with only 250 test pairs, and dynamic objects are mostly excluded. The benchmark may therefore underrepresent real deployment conditions where people, changing illumination, partial overlap, and moving distractors are common.

The robotic demonstration is illustrative but not strong evidence. It appears to be a single controlled table-cleaning setup with extra RealSense alignment, so it does not substantially validate the generality of the method in robotics.

Several presentation choices make the contribution feel overstated: claims such as 'state-of-the-art' and large-margin improvements are technically supported by the included tables, but the comparison set and forgiving metric make the practical significance less clear. A more cautious framing around the benchmark contribution would be more persuasive.

strengths: I assess the paper primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with a companion algorithmic baseline, rather than only as an Algorithms/General paper. Under that lens, the contribution is timely and useful: multiview object-level change detection is under-served, and SceneDiff provides 350 real video pairs, 1009 changed objects, instance masks, change-type labels, per-view and per-scene evaluation, and clear annotation tooling.
weaknesses: The benchmark, while valuable, is still moderate in scale and appears to have limited discussion of annotation quality control, inter-annotator agreement, privacy/consent, and licensing beyond avoiding identity information and promising release upon acceptance. These details matter for a dataset paper.

The method is a well-engineered composition of strong pretrained components (pi3, SAM, DINO) rather than a deeply novel learning formulation. This is acceptable for a benchmark/baseline paper, but the algorithmic novelty is incremental.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat constrained. Some competing methods are adapted under unfavorable conditions or cannot support the proposed per-scene metric, while the VLM baseline is quite weak. The large margins are encouraging, but a stronger set of multiview/open-vocabulary or tracking/reconstruction baselines would make the empirical case more definitive.

The evaluation protocol intentionally converts masks/boxes to points and tolerates duplicate predictions. This makes comparison broad and pragmatic, but it does not fully assess segmentation quality or penalize over-fragmentation as strongly as some downstream uses would require.

Absolute performance remains far from solved, especially on SD-K and change-type classification: e.g., per-scene APtype is 25.5 on SD-V and 12.2 on SD-K. The paper acknowledges this, but it limits the immediate practical robustness of the proposed method.

The approach is computationally heavy and brittle in known regimes: average inference is reported around 159 seconds per sequence pair, and failures occur with low overlap, lighting shifts, repetitive clutter, dynamic objects unless masked, and reconstruction failures. These limitations are meaningful for robotics and monitoring deployments.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored computer vision problem: object-level change detection from before/after videos captured along different trajectories. I would assess it primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with an accompanying applied/system method, rather than as a purely algorithmic paper; under that lens, the benchmark and evaluation protocol are substantial contributions.

SceneDiff Benchmark appears useful and timely: 350 real-world video pairs, 50 scenes, indoor/outdoor coverage, 1009 changed objects, dense instance masks across visible frames, consistent cross-view IDs, and metrics spanning per-pixel, per-view object, and scene-level object AP. The scene-level metric is especially well motivated because it evaluates whether a system identifies physical changed objects rather than repeated per-frame detections.

The method is technically sensible: it combines joint geometry estimation, co-visible frame pairing, SAM regions, DINO features, asymmetric depth reprojection, 3D score aggregation, and cross-view instance association. While many components are borrowed, their integration is appropriate for the task and the design choices are clearly connected to the problem's failure modes.

The experimental evidence is broad. The paper evaluates on the proposed benchmark, RC-3D, PASLCD, and ChangeSim; compares to 2D/3D change detection, 3DGS-based, and VLM baselines; includes finetuned baselines where possible; and reports ablations over geometry models, visual features, cue combinations, thresholds, runtime, failure cases, and stricter change-type-aware obj/sc AP.

Results are convincing relative to existing methods. On SceneDiff, the proposed method strongly improves over baselines across pixel, per-image object, and scene-level object metrics, and on RC-3D it improves AP50 over prior 3D change detection methods. The paper is also honest that absolute scene-level AP remains low, especially on the kitchen subset, which supports the benchmark's difficulty.

The supplementary material improves reproducibility and trust: it describes baseline adaptations, annotation workflow, data collection instructions, runtime, hyperparameter sensitivity, and representative failure cases. The planned release of dataset, annotation tool, evaluation code, and codebase would make the work valuable to the community.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. The method is mostly a well-engineered composition of recent foundation models and geometry/feature matching heuristics, with several thresholds and post-processing steps. This is acceptable for a benchmark/system contribution, but it limits the paper's claim as a new method.

Absolute performance remains far from solving the proposed task: obj/sc AP is 22.8 on SD-V and 10.6 on SD-K, dropping to 18.5 and 7.7 under change-type-aware evaluation. This is not a fatal flaw, since the benchmark is meant to be challenging, but it means the practical reliability claims should be kept modest.

The dataset is promising but still somewhat limited in scale and diversity for a benchmark intended to define a new task: 350 video pairs from 50 scenes, with data collection guidelines that encourage similar coverage and avoid dynamic people/limbs. This may underrepresent many real deployment conditions such as crowds, outdoor temporal variation, severe weather/lighting changes, and large structural changes.

Annotation quality control is not fully established. The paper describes SAM2-assisted annotation and review, but does not report inter-annotator agreement, independent audit statistics, mask correction rates, or error estimates. For a benchmark paper, stronger evidence of label consistency would be valuable.

Some baseline comparisons require substantial adaptation, and the fairness is not always airtight. Box methods are converted to masks with SAM, 3DGS-based methods are given regressed camera parameters and modified evaluation pipelines, and the VLM baseline uses manual text-to-ground-truth matching to isolate recognition. These choices are mostly explained, but they make the headline margins somewhat dependent on implementation details.

The method depends heavily on large pretrained models, especially geometry estimation and SAM/DINO-style features. Failure cases show sensitivity to limited overlap, lighting changes, cluttered repetitive objects, and dynamic content unless an external dynamic mask is supplied. Runtime is also relatively high at about 159 seconds per sequence pair, mostly due to segmentation.

The practical/societal aspects are thin. Data collection guidelines mention avoiding identity information, but the paper does not deeply discuss privacy, consent, dataset licensing, or potential surveillance uses of change detection. This matters for real-world video benchmarks involving indoor and outdoor spaces.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored problem: object-level change detection from before/after videos captured along different trajectories. This is a useful setting for robotics, inspection, and inventory applications, and the proposed per-image and per-scene metrics are well motivated.

The SceneDiff benchmark is potentially valuable. It includes real videos, instance-level object masks, change types, cross-view object identity, indoor/outdoor scenes, and both manually collected and egocentric kitchen data. The annotation tool and evaluation protocol would be useful if released cleanly.

The method is technically plausible and reasonably modular, combining geometry registration, SAM-based regions, DINO features, reprojection cues, and cross-frame association. The ablations indicate that geometry choice and feature cues matter, and the paper includes some failure cases and sensitivity analyses.

The results show consistent gains over adapted baselines on the proposed benchmark and reasonable transfer to RC-3D, PASLCD, and ChangeSim, suggesting that the pipeline captures useful signal beyond a single dataset.
weaknesses: The algorithmic contribution is limited. The method is largely an assembly of recent foundation models and standard operations: feed-forward geometry, SAM regions, DINO features, reprojection differences, thresholding, and greedy association. The paper’s novelty rests more on problem framing and benchmarking than on a substantial new vision algorithm.

The empirical case is weakened by low absolute performance on the central benchmark. The most important metric, obj/sc AP, is only 22.8 on SD-V and 10.6 on SD-K, and change-type-aware performance drops further to 18.5 and 7.7. These numbers suggest that the task remains largely unsolved, but the paper’s claims about practical utility and robust object-level change detection feel stronger than the evidence supports.

Baseline comparisons are difficult to trust as decisive evidence. Many baselines are heavily adapted, use different output types, are converted through SAM, are evaluated under different metrics, or are given modified inputs such as the authors’ regressed poses. Only a small subset of baselines produce scene-level object tracks, so the strongest claimed metric is not broadly comparable.

The benchmark, while interesting, appears modest in scale for a dataset paper: 350 sequence pairs from 50 scenes and 1009 changed objects. The paper does not provide enough evidence about annotation quality, inter-annotator agreement, consistency of object identities, or error rates from SAM2-assisted propagation. Since the dataset is a major contribution, this validation gap is important.

The evaluation protocol introduces several design choices that may favor the proposed pipeline, including SAM-based mask conversion, dynamic thresholding, view pairing, object aggregation, and change-type-agnostic obj/sc AP as the main metric. More independent or standardized evaluation would be needed to establish the benchmark’s reliability.

The robotic demonstration is anecdotal and does not substantially validate downstream usefulness. It appears to be a single tabletop example with extra RealSense alignment, rather than a systematic robotic experiment.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing from the manuscript alone. The method depends on multiple large, rapidly changing pretrained systems, including recent or future-facing models such as DINOv3, π3, and SAM3, and the dataset is promised for release upon acceptance. Runtime is also substantial at about 159 seconds per sequence pair.

The limitations section is honest but incomplete. It notes ambiguity, pose failures, and unsupported semantic/surface changes, but gives limited quantitative characterization of failure modes such as dynamic objects, lighting shifts, low overlap, repeated similar objects, and clutter, all of which are central to the claimed application scenarios.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-served vision problem: object-level change detection across different camera trajectories. The benchmark contribution is substantial, with 350 real video pairs, dense instance-level annotations, added/removed/moved labels, and evaluation at pixel, per-view object, and scene-level object consistency granularity.

The proposed SceneDiff method is technically sensible and well matched to the task: joint geometry regression, view-pair selection, SAM regions, DINO features, asymmetric depth/feature reprojection, and multi-view instance association form a coherent training-free pipeline rather than an ad hoc baseline.

Empirical evidence is strong overall. The method improves substantially over adapted two-view, 3DGS-based, and VLM baselines on the new benchmark, and also performs competitively or better on RC-3D, PASLCD, and ChangeSim. The paper includes useful ablations over cues, feature backbones, geometry models, thresholds, and failure modes.

The benchmark framing is particularly valuable for the community. The obj/sc AP metric highlights a real limitation of per-frame change detection: detecting the same physical changed object consistently across views. This is a meaningful contribution even independent of the method.

The manuscript is clear and well organized, with helpful qualitative figures, dataset statistics, baseline implementation details, runtime reporting, hyperparameter sensitivity, and explicit limitations. The robotics demonstration, while small, illustrates practical relevance.
weaknesses: Although the benchmark is valuable, its scale remains moderate: 350 video pairs and 1009 changed objects, with 50 physical scenes. This is enough to establish a useful benchmark, but it may not fully support broad claims about general real-world deployment across construction, warehouses, disaster response, and other domains.

The absolute scene-level performance is still low: obj/sc AP is 22.8 on SD-V and 10.6 on SD-K, dropping further under change-type-aware evaluation. This suggests the task remains far from solved, and the method should be interpreted as a strong baseline rather than a robust general solution.

The main obj/sc AP metric is change-type agnostic, even though classifying added/removed/moved objects is part of the stated task. The stricter supplementary metric is appreciated, but the main presentation somewhat understates errors in change classification.

Reproducibility depends heavily on several large and very recent foundation models, including geometry, segmentation, and feature models. If any of these models or their exact versions are unavailable, expensive, or change over time, reproducing the reported numbers may be difficult despite the promised code release.

Some baseline comparisons require nontrivial adaptations, including using the authors' regressed camera parameters for 3DGS methods, converting boxes to masks with SAM, manually matching VLM text outputs to ground-truth labels, and special filtering for CYWS-3D. These choices are documented and often reasonable, but they make the fairness and comparability of all baselines harder to audit.

The dataset annotation protocol is described, but the paper gives limited evidence on annotation quality, ambiguity handling, or inter-annotator agreement. For a benchmark paper, stronger validation of annotation consistency would increase confidence.

The method is relatively slow at about 159 seconds per sequence pair on an A40 and can fail under limited overlap, strong lighting changes, repetitive clutter, dynamic content without masks, and pose-estimation failures. These are well acknowledged, but they constrain practical use.
